notes.meaning: God had stopped the terrible plague at the threshing floor of Ornan and accepted David's sacrifice with fire from heaven. David recognized that the Lord had chosen this very spot on Mount Moriah for Israel's future temple and the main altar for offerings. Even though the tabernacle tent was still at Gibeon, David knew God was now setting up this new permanent home for His worship.

David ordered the resident foreigners living in Israel to be assembled to help prepare materials for the temple. These people were descendants of Canaanite nations who lived under Israel's rule and were called on for public work projects. David put them to work cutting and shaping large stones to build the foundation and walls of God's house.

David gathered huge amounts of iron to make nails, hinges, and metal clamps to join the heavy wooden gates. He also collected bronze in such vast quantities that the workers could not even weigh it all. Since Israel had subdued the Philistines, who once tightly controlled iron tools and weapons, David was now able to provide strong building metals in abundance.

David secured countless cedar logs through trade with the coastal cities of Tyre and Sidon. The Phoenicians were famous for harvesting timber from Mount Lebanon and sending it down by sea in exchange for Israel's grain and oil. This strong, fragrant wood was ideal for roof beams, ceilings, and paneling inside the temple.

David knew his son Solomon was still young and lacked experience with such a massive project. Because the Lord's house needed to be grand and bring honor to God among all nations, David took it upon himself to gather materials beforehand. Even though David could not build the temple himself, he worked hard before he died so the work could succeed.

As he neared the end of his life, David called Solomon in for a solemn meeting. He passed on the sacred duty of building the temple to his son and officially commissioned him for the task. David wanted Solomon to understand that this project was a divine calling from God, not just a personal family idea.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern scholars view David's farewell address here as a literary composition crafted by the Chronicler to highlight David's spiritual vision rather than a word-for-word transcript.

notes.meaning: David shared his heart with his son, telling Solomon how deeply he had longed to build the temple himself. Years earlier, David had wanted to build a permanent home for God's ark to honor the Lord's name. It had been his earnest desire to serve God in this way out of love for Him.

God told David that he could not build the temple because his reign had been full of warfare and bloodshed. While David's battles were fought at God's command to defend Israel, God wanted His temple to represent peace rather than war. David's life as a warrior meant he was not the right person to build this holy sanctuary.

God promised David that his son Solomon would be a man of rest, free from the wars David had fought. Solomon's name comes from the Hebrew word for peace, and the Lord promised quiet rest for Israel throughout his reign. This season of national peace would give Solomon the time, energy, and resources needed to focus on building the temple.

God appointed Solomon as the one who would build His temple and promised to treat him as a son. The Lord also promised that David's royal line would be established over Israel forever. Christian teachers have long seen this ultimate promise pointing beyond Solomon to Jesus Christ, whose kingdom truly lasts forever.

David prayed a blessing over Solomon, asking the Lord to be with him and give him success in building the temple. He reminded Solomon that God had already spoken this promise over his life. Knowing God has called us to a task gives us confidence to step forward and carry it out.

David asked God to grant Solomon wisdom and discernment when he stepped up to lead the nation. The greatest purpose of this wisdom was not just political skill, but the ability to obey God's law faithfully. Good leadership and true prosperity begin with listening to God and following His directions.

David warned Solomon that lasting success depended on carefully obeying the laws God gave through Moses. He echoed the famous words once spoken to Joshua, telling Solomon to be strong and courageous without fear. Doing God's work requires moral courage that rests on trusting God's promises.

Through seasons of hard struggle and military campaigns, David amassed a staggering supply of gold, silver, bronze, iron, wood, and stone. He laid all these resources before Solomon, while generously encouraging his son to add his own gifts to the work. David showed that devotion to God involves offering our best efforts and treasures to His service.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars understand the extraordinarily large sums of gold and silver as round numbers used rhetorically to express great wealth, rather than literal modern weights.

notes.meaning: In addition to gathering materials, David had organized a massive workforce ready for Solomon to direct. This included stonecutters to quarry rock, masons to build walls, carpenters to shape timber, and craftsmen skilled in every trade. David made sure his son had both the supplies and the skilled hands needed to do the job well.

David pointed out the countless craftsmen ready to work with gold, silver, bronze, and iron. He then urged Solomon to get started without delay as soon as he came to the throne, praying that the Lord would be with him. God's promised presence is the best reason to rise up and begin the work.

David turned to all the tribal princes and leaders of Israel and commanded them to support Solomon. He knew that even a gifted young king could not manage such an enormous project without the full cooperation of the nation's leaders. David asked them to provide wise counsel, practical help, and oversight for the builders.

David reminded the leaders of God's great goodness in giving Israel victory and peace along all its borders. Because the Lord had brought an end to the fighting and made the land secure, the nation had the peace and wealth needed to build. David urged them to show gratitude for this God-given rest by devoting their energy to the Lord's house.

David called on the leaders to dedicate their hearts fully to seeking the Lord by helping build His sanctuary, or sacred worship place. The goal was to give the ark of the covenant—the sacred chest that represented God's presence—a permanent and honored home. Seeking God was not just an inner feeling, but active obedience that showed honor to His name.
